values.goal: Understand stage inputs and mathematics in GLSL ES, and implement, diagnose, and compare visual effects in WebGL2.
values.capstone: An experiment with a pointer-controlled procedural surface and postprocessing, compilation recovery, and quality and cost records

values.title: Vertex and Fragment
values.prerequisites: Vector operations and creating WebGL programs
values.environment: The existing glsl-01 preview is a starting point. It does not replace implementation or verification of the full subsequent assignment. This document-guided exercise requires your own implementation using WebGL2 and GLSL ES 3.00 in a separate localhost project. First check the GLSL version of existing examples and avoid mixing in 1.00 syntax.
values.concepts.0.title: Stage Roles
values.concepts.0.explanation: The vertex shader computes the clip position and values to pass to the next stage. The fragment shader produces output for a pixel candidate from interpolated inputs.
values.concepts.1.title: Version Contract
values.concepts.1.explanation: Distinguish WebGL1 GLSL ES 1.00 syntax from WebGL2 3.00 syntax. In 3.00, use #version 300 es on the first line, in/out, and an explicit fragment output.
values.outcomes.0: Explain the responsibilities of shader stages.
values.steps.0: Create a webgl2 context in main.js and separate the vertex.glsl and fragment.glsl sources.
values.steps.1: Connect a vertex shader that only returns positions and a fixed-color fragment shader using compileShader and linkProgram.
values.steps.2: Introduce a syntax error in one source and an interface error between the two stages separately, and compare the logs.
values.variables.0.name: fragment color
values.variables.0.expected: Expect only the output color to change, while vertex positions remain unchanged.
values.criteria.0: Print compile and link logs separately.
values.criteria.1: Do not mix attribute, varying, or gl_FragColor into GLSL ES 3.00 sources.
values.questions.0: When can one fragment differ from one screen pixel?
values.questions.1: Why can linking fail even when both shaders compile individually?
values.references.0.title: GLSL ES 3.00 Specification

values.title: Scalar and Vector Types
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and records from Unit 1. Before experimenting with Scalar and Vector Types, preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs.
values.environment: First check the execution scope guidance on the example screen. The following describes the environment needed to extend the assignment in a separate project. This document-guided exercise requires your own implementation using WebGL2 and GLSL ES 3.00 in a separate localhost project. First check the GLSL version of existing examples and avoid mixing in 1.00 syntax.
values.concepts.0.title: Explicit Types
values.concepts.0.explanation: float, int, and bool serve different purposes, and relying on implicit conversions can easily cause errors. Use constructors to express the intended types and component counts.
values.concepts.1.title: Vector Operations
values.concepts.1.explanation: Vector multiplication is component-wise, while dot produces one scalar. Check the result type and meaning even when the notation looks similar.
values.outcomes.1: Predict the results of vector operations.
values.steps.0: Write vec2, vec3, and vec4 constructor and swizzle examples in types.glsl.
values.steps.1: Apply component-wise multiplication and dot separately to the input color, and display them in two screen regions.
values.steps.2: Supply an incorrect component count, locate the line in the compile log, and fix it.
values.variables.0.name: Calculation method
values.variables.0.expected: Expect per-channel values from the former and identical gray channels from the latter.
values.criteria.0: Compare CPU predictions with shader output for both calculations.
values.criteria.1: Record one invalid-constructor error and its correction.
values.questions.0: Can you assign to a swizzle that repeats the same component?
values.questions.1: What types do length and normalization return?
values.references.0.title: GLSL ES 3.00 Specification

values.title: Precision and Numeric Range
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and records from Unit 2. Before experimenting with Precision and Numeric Range, preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs.
values.environment: First check the execution scope guidance on the example screen. The following describes the environment needed to extend the assignment in a separate project. This document-guided exercise requires your own implementation using WebGL2 and GLSL ES 3.00 in a separate localhost project. First check the GLSL version of existing examples and avoid mixing in 1.00 syntax.
values.concepts.0.title: Precision
values.concepts.0.explanation: A precision qualifier relates to the representable range and accuracy. In particular, do not omit the default float precision declaration in the fragment shader.
values.concepts.1.title: Large Coordinates
values.concepts.1.explanation: Adding a small change to a large number may fail to represent that change. Compare moving coordinates to a local reference frame to reduce the range of calculations.
values.outcomes.1: Explore numeric problems with large coordinates.
values.steps.1: Declare highp float in fragment.glsl and add a small sin variation to a large offset.
values.steps.2: Compare the patterns before and after removing the offset at the same screen size.
values.variables.0.name: Coordinate offset
values.variables.0.expected: Expect possible jitter or clumping in the pattern because small differences may be difficult to represent.
values.criteria.0: Record the device's highp and mediump ranges and precision.
values.criteria.1: Save images of both offsets at the same time point.
values.questions.0: Does highp eliminate every numeric problem?
values.questions.1: What improves when large world coordinates are moved to a camera-relative frame?
values.references.0.title: GLSL ES 3.00 Specification
